# A mechanism for substrate quality control in outer membrane protein assembly

**Authors:** Ashton N. Combs; Anna Konovalova; Thomas J. Silhavy

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544 | bDepartment of Microbiology and Molecular Genetics, McGovern Medical School, The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, Houston, TX 77030

## Abstract

The assembly of β-barrel proteins into the outer membrane (OM) of Gram-negative bacteria is catalyzed by the β-barrel assembly machine (Bam) complex, which consists of two essential proteins, the BamA β-barrel and the lipoprotein BamD, and three nonessential lipoproteins BamBCE. While it is well-established that BamD serves an essential role in regulating the activity of BamA, the physiological reasons underpinning the need for BamD-mediated regulation of β-barrel assembly are unclear. Here, we demonstrate that BamD-mediated regulation of BamA functions as a mechanism of substrate quality control that ensures the efficient assembly of β-barrel proteins into the OM. Through the use of substrate C-terminal fragments and multiple alleles of bamA and bamD that prevent effective regulation of BamA by BamD, we show that BamD activity is necessary to prevent the accumulation of defective β-barrel substrates on BamA. Notably, these bamAD alleles all confer resistance to the Bam complex inhibitor MRL-494 in a manner that correlates with the degree to which BamD activity is bypassed, suggesting that MRL-494 inhibits β-barrel assembly by disrupting BamD-mediated conformational changes in BamA. We further show that BamD activity functions to prevent the uptake of toxic small molecules across the OM through a mechanism that functionally overlaps with that of the substrate quality control protein Skp. Collectively, these results not only establish that BamD, like Skp, functions to ensure proper quality control of β-barrel substrates but also demonstrate the importance of substrate quality control functions in maintaining the integrity of the OM permeability barrier.

## INTRODUCTION

The outer membrane (OM) of Gram-negative bacteria, such as Escherichia coli, is an essential organelle that functions as a permeability barrier, lends mechanical strength to the cell envelope, and influences cell shape (1–5). The defining features of this distinctive membrane include its asymmetric distribution of lipids, with phospholipids in the inner leaflet and the glycolipid lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet, and its exceptionally high protein content (1, 2). Nearly all transmembrane proteins in the OM are β-barrel outer membrane proteins (OMPs) that are composed of antiparallel β-strands wrapped into a cylindrical array (1, 2). Diverse and essential roles performed by β-barrel OMPs are integral to each of the major functions of the Gram-negative OM, contributing to the selective permeability, mechanical strength, and organization of the OM as well as cell shape (1–4, 6, 7).

The folding and insertion of β-barrel OMPs into the OM is catalyzed by the β-barrel assembly machine (Bam) complex which contains the β-barrel OMP BamA and four accessory lipoproteins BamBCDE (8, 9). Of these five proteins, only BamA and BamD are essential for viability (8, 10). BamA alone is sufficient to catalyze the assembly of OMPs into the OM (11), suggesting that the roles of the lipoproteins BamBCDE in OMP assembly are regulatory. Such regulatory functions are necessary for the Bam complex to facilitate the efficient folding and insertion of numerous, diverse β-barrel substrates (8, 11–19).

While the mechanism by which the Bam complex catalyzes the folding and insertion of β-barrel OMPs into the OM remains an active area of investigation, several conserved features of the assembly process have been established. Substrate recruitment to the Bam complex is facilitated by BamD (13), which binds a conserved, semi-degenerate motif known as the β-signal that lies near the substrate C terminus (20). The C-terminal β-strand of the substrate is then engaged by the N-terminal β-strand of the BamA β-barrel, creating a strong, rigid interaction between substrate and machine through the formation of an asymmetric hybrid barrel (21, 22). BamA then catalyzes substrate folding in a C-to-N-terminal manner (21), though the precise mechanism by which this occurs remains controversial (21–32). While it is clear that BamD serves an essential role in regulating the activity of BamA (11–16), the physiological reasons underpinning the need for BamD-mediated regulation of OMP assembly remain unclear.

As the Bam complex both performs an essential cellular process and is exposed at the cell surface, it represents an attractive target for antibiotics (33–36). Identifying the general quality control mechanisms that ensure rapid and efficient Bam-catalyzed assembly of β-barrel substrates could therefore inform the development of strategies to better combat Gram-negative pathogens. While we previously identified one such substrate quality control mechanism mediated by the periplasmic chaperone Skp (37), its removal seemingly imposes little physiological consequence under laboratory conditions, even in the presence of slow-folding β-barrel substrates (38). Given these observations, along with the fact that β-barrel OMPs are both highly abundant and integral to bacterial physiology (1–4, 6, 7), it stands to reason that additional general substrate quality control mechanisms that enable efficient Bam complex activity may exist.

Here, we demonstrate that BamD-mediated regulation of BamA functions as a mechanism of substrate quality control to ensure the proper assembly of β-barrel OMPs by the Bam complex. We show that bypassing BamD activity phenocopies the removal of Skp, producing comparable substrate quality control defects that are conferred through the same basic mechanism. By screening for mutations in bamD that confer resistance to the Bam complex inhibitor MRL-494, we identify an allele of bamD that is similarly defective in substrate quality control due to its inability to form a single, direct interaction with BamA, directly implicating BamD in both the substrate quality control process and the mechanism of resistance to MRL-494. We further demonstrate that the ability of a given bamA allele to tolerate reductions in BamD activity is predictive of both the magnitude of substrate quality control defects and level of MRL-494 resistance conferred. Lastly, we show that BamD activity prevents toxic small molecules from penetrating the OM and that this activity functionally overlaps with that of Skp. Together, our results establish that BamD-mediated regulation of BamA, like Skp, functions in the quality control of β-barrel substrates during OMP assembly and demonstrate the importance of substrate quality control functions in maintaining OM integrity.

## RESULTS

### Use of substrate C-terminal fragments to identify mechanisms of quality control

Previously, we have utilized slow-folding β-barrel substrates as a tool to deliberately perturb the OMP assembly process and identify general mechanisms of substrate quality control. Such efforts revealed a specific role for the periplasmic chaperone Skp in facilitating the direct removal and degradation of assembly-compromised substrates from the Bam complex (38). Slow-folding β-barrel substrates that have stalled during assembly and have not yet membrane integrated are removed from the Bam complex by Skp and are subsequently targeted for degradation by the periplasmic protease DegP, a process that results in the degradation of both Skp and its bound OMP substrate (38). As the slow-folding β-barrel substrates that we utilized to identify this mechanism of substrate quality control are both assembly-competent and exhibit relatively mild folding defects, they are readily assembled in the absence of Skp; simply deleting skp allows these slow-folding β-barrel substrates to reside on the Bam complex long enough to eventually complete assembly (38).

To more stringently perturb the process of OMP assembly and facilitate the identification of additional potential mechanisms of quality control, we wished to design a series of OMP substrates that were far more defective in assembly than the slow-folding β-barrel OMPs we have previously utilized. Such slow-folding OMPs included extracellular loop deletions that impart folding defects through the slowed formation of β-hairpins at the point of the deletion (38). As OMP assembly by the Bam complex proceeds directionally in a C-to-N-terminal manner, deletion of a substrate extracellular loop causes OMPs to stall at discrete points in their assembly based on how distal the extracellular loop deletion lies from the C terminus (21). Wanting to employ a similarly systematic approach in substrate design, we reasoned that use of substrate C-terminal fragments would afford a series of OMPs that would not only stall at distinct points during folding but could also be designed such that they might be terminally defective in their assembly. Given that substrates lacking an extracellular loop are expected to exhibit folding defects at a point during assembly in which they have assembled an odd number of β-strands (21), we reasoned that substrate C-terminal fragments encoding the same number of strands would not only be expected to stall at the same points in assembly as their analogous extracellular loop deletions, but would also lack any of the remaining N-terminal protein sequence needed to fully complete assembly. Such C-terminal fragments, once folded, would also be expected to contain N- and C-terminal β-strands that are arranged parallel to one another, which could additionally prevent efficient hydrogen bond formation between N- and C- substrate termini, a process that is normally required to facilitate barrel closure and substrate release from the Bam complex (21, 24). We chose to utilize the β-barrel domain of BamA as a substrate, as many of the sequence determinants important for BamA assembly—in addition to its general folding trajectory—have been well-characterized genetically and biochemically (20, 21, 23, 39).

Substrate C-terminal fragments were designed to encode between 1–15 β-strands of the BamA β-barrel domain such that they would be expected to stall at the same points in assembly as their corresponding extracellular loop deletions once folded (i.e., containing an odd number of β-strands) (Fig. 1A) and constructed using the arabinose-inducible vector pBAD18 (40) to afford tight, inducible regulation of substrates that could potentially be toxic. Of note, the β-signal, which facilitates the binding of nascent OMP substrates to the Bam complex, is approximately 30 amino acids removed from the absolute C terminus in BamA (20, 39); thus, a construct encoding only the C-terminal–most β-strand of BamA (i.e., BamAβ1) lacks a β-signal (Fig. 1A) and additionally serves as a control for substrates that should not efficiently engage with the assembly machinery. Following induction of expression by plating on media containing arabinose, substrate C-terminal fragments exhibited two distinct plating efficiencies when overexpressed in an otherwise wild-type genetic background (Fig. 1B). As expected, a substrate containing only the C-terminal–most β-strand of BamA (BamAβ1) showed no reduction in plating efficiency when induced with arabinose (Fig. 1B). Substrates containing 3, 5, 7, or 9 β-strands of BamA (BamAβ3, BamAβ5, BamAβ7, and BamAβ9) similarly showed only minimal or no reduction in plating efficiency when expressed (Fig. 1B), suggesting that these substrates are either only loosely engaged by the assembly machinery or are handled efficiently by existing substrate quality control mechanisms (e.g., Skp and/or DegP). Substrate C-terminal fragments encoding 11, 13, or 15 β-strands of BamA (BamAβ11, BamAβ13, and BamAβ15), however, conferred substantial toxicity when expressed, as indicated by a significant reduction in plating efficiency relative to the uninduced fucose control (Fig. 1B). These results suggest that the substrate quality control mechanisms monitoring late-stage folding intermediates, if any, are insufficient to maintain cellular viability when challenged with a high volume of defective substrate, at least at the level of expression achieved using pBAD18-based vectors.

As a proof of principle, we then wished to determine whether the substrates that were both capable of being engaged by assembly machinery and showed only minimal or no reduction in plating efficiency (BamAβ3, BamAβ5, BamAβ7, and BamAβ9) were being acted upon by known mechanisms of substrate quality control. As OMP substrates that have stalled during folding and have not yet membrane integrated are removed from the Bam complex and targeted for degradation by Skp (38), a genetic interaction should exist between defective substrates that are efficiently engaged by the assembly machinery and skp; removal of skp should result in the accumulation of these substrates on the assembly machinery and ultimately exacerbate the toxicity associated with their expression. Indeed, while the plating efficiencies of strains expressing substrates BamAβ3 and BamAβ5 were unaffected by skp deletion (Fig. 1C), the toxicities of substrates BamAβ7 and BamAβ9 were significantly increased upon skp removal (Fig. 1C). As would be expected, the plating efficiencies of strains expressing substrates that either should not efficiently engage with the assembly machinery (BamAβ1) or proceed far enough into the assembly process to confer toxicity even in a wild-type background (BamAβ11, BamAβ13, and BamAβ15) were largely unaffected by skp deletion (Fig. 1C). These results suggest that while substrates BamAβ3 and BamAβ5 may only be loosely engaged by the assembly machinery and might not require Skp to prevent their accumulation, substrates BamAβ7 and BamAβ9 are capable of proceeding far enough in the assembly process such that they require Skp to facilitate their removal from the Bam complex; removal of skp causes BamAβ7 and BamAβ9 to accumulate on the assembly machinery, which inhibits normal OMP assembly by the Bam complex and ultimately results in lethality. Together, these results demonstrate that substrate C-terminal fragments, particularly substrates BamAβ7 and BamAβ9 in the case of BamA, can be utilized as a tool to identify general mechanisms of substrate quality control during OMP assembly by the Bam complex.

### BamAE470K bypasses a normal mechanism of substrate quality control and phenocopies Δskp

It is well established that the lipoprotein BamD regulates the activity of BamA and that this regulatory function is essential for proper OMP assembly (11–16). Conformational coordination of both BamA and BamD is required for assembly to proceed (13, 14, 41), and substrates that fail to induce BamD-mediated conformational changes in BamA are removed from the Bam complex by Skp and ultimately degraded by DegP (13, 38). Given these observations, it stands to reason that BamD, like Skp, may also function in substrate quality control. However, direct evidence demonstrating such a function is lacking, largely complicated by the essential nature of BamD for normal OMP assembly (10).

We previously identified and characterized a gain-of-function allele of bamA, bamAE470K, that confers resistance to the Bam complex inhibitor MRL-494 (33). bamAE470K also bypasses the essentiality of BamD (12), likely by favoring a conformation of BamA that is normally promoted by BamD. We therefore reasoned that if bamAE470K bypasses the essential requirement for BamD in OMP assembly, then bamAE470K may also bypass any existing, BamD-mediated substrate quality control functions. Strikingly, expression of BamA substrate C-terminal fragments in a bamAE470K genetic background phenocopied Δskp for all constructed substrates (Fig. 1D and SI Appendix, Fig. S1); bamAE470K, like Δskp, only significantly increased the toxicities of substrates BamAβ7 and BamAβ9, and did so to a comparable degree (Fig. 1D). Furthermore, expression of BamAβ7 or BamAβ9 in a bamAE470K Δskp genetic background resulted in a greater reduction in plating efficiency than either single mutation alone (Fig. 1D). Introduction of the bamAW776Q β-signal mutation—which reduces the affinity of substrate BamA for BamD (20)—into bamAβ7 completely suppressed the plating defects conferred by Δskp and/or bamAE470K (Fig. 1E), thus demonstrating that efficient engagement of BamAβ7 by the Bam complex is required for these plating defects to occur. These results suggest that while BamAE470K does not require BamD-mediated regulation, it can no longer undergo a normal mechanism of substrate quality control in a manner similar to Δskp; in either a bamAE470K or Δskp genetic background, substrates BamAβ7 and BamAβ9 accumulate on the assembly machinery, resulting in the inhibition of OMP assembly by the Bam complex and ultimately cellular lethality.

To directly demonstrate that the defects in substrate quality control conferred by either Δskp or bamAE470K were occurring through similar mechanisms, we utilized in vivo, site-specific photocrosslinking to determine whether each mutation indeed causes an increased accumulation of defective substrate on BamA. Upon incorporation of the unnatural amino acid p-benzoyl-L-phenylalanine (pBpa) into assembly machinery BamA and irradiation with ultraviolet (UV) light, substrates residing close enough to the site of pBpa incorporation can be covalently crosslinked to BamA, and the resulting BamA–substrate crosslinked adducts can then be detected as a high-molecular-weight product by immunoblotting (21–23, 42). We incorporated pBpa at residue S439 of assembly machinery BamA, as this residue lies directly adjacent to the BamA lateral gate—a region well-established to form a strong interaction with substrates (21, 22, 24–26) that is integral to the assembly mechanism—and has previously been shown to productively crosslink to many defective and native substrates (21–23). Accumulation of substrate BamAβ7 at the BamA lateral gate was assessed in wild-type, Δskp, bamAE470K, and bamAE470K Δskp genetic backgrounds following a brief (2 min) induction of substrate to minimize the toxic effects that occur following BamAβ7 expression. As expected given our previous genetic data (38), deletion of skp resulted in increased crosslinking of BamAβ7 to residue S439 near the lateral gate of BamA, in a manner that was both UV-dependent and specific to the S439 amber mutation (bamAS439Am) that enables pBpa incorporation (Fig. 1F). Crucially, however, bamAE470K also conferred increased crosslinking of BamAβ7 to residue S439 of assembly machinery BamA, and the same was true for a bamAE470K Δskp double mutant (Fig. 1F). These results directly demonstrate that the Δskp and bamAE470K mutations result in similar outcomes for substrate BamAβ7; either mutation confers defects in substrate quality control that result in the increased accumulation of BamAβ7 on assembly machinery BamA. Thus, the toxicities associated with the expression of substrate C-terminal fragments in Δskp and bamAE470K genetic backgrounds are conferred through similar mechanisms. We conclude that BamAE470K bypasses a normal mechanism of substrate quality control in a manner that phenocopies Δskp.

### A mutation in bamD confers both MRL-494 resistance and defects in substrate quality control

If the substrate quality control defects conferred by bamAE470K are indeed a result of bypassing BamD function, then there should exist an allele of bamD that phenocopies bamAE470K. As previously mentioned, we initially isolated bamAE470K due to its ability to confer resistance to the Bam complex inhibitor MRL-494 (33). Therefore, we reasoned that there might exist mutations in bamD that are sufficient to confer MRL-494 resistance.

To this end, we screened an NNK degenerate, single-codon mutagenesis library of plasmid-borne bamD for mutations that conferred increased MRL-494 resistance (Fig. 2A) using the same general procedure we previously utilized to identify bamAE470K (33). Twelve unique, MRL-494-resistant mutant pools sequenced across three independently conducted screens identified the same single mutation in bamD, bamDR188P. Residue R188 of BamD is notable as it is one of the few BamD residues that directly interacts with BamA; residue R188 of BamD and residue D481 of BamA constitute a salt bridge that facilitates a direct, electrostatic interaction between BamD and periplasmic loop 2 of the β-barrel domain of BamA (Fig. 2B) (43). Such an interaction is of particular interest as electrostatic interactions between BamA and BamD are well-known to be critical for regulating the conformational dynamics of these two essential Bam complex components during OMP assembly (14, 15, 41).

We then constructed a strain harboring bamDR188P at the native chromosomal locus to determine whether bamDR188P in single-copy was sufficient to confer MRL-494 resistance, using bamAE470K as a positive control. As was true for bamAE470K expressed from an ectopic chromosomal locus (attTn7) (33), bamAE470K reconstructed at its native chromosomal locus conferred >4-fold resistance to MRL-494 and permitted growth to the limit of MRL-494 solubility in minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) assays (Fig. 2C). bamDR188P in single-copy at its native chromosomal locus provided 2-fold increased resistance to MRL-494, confirming that there exists a mutation in bamD that is sufficient to confer MRL-494 resistance (Fig. 2C). Given that our identified variant specifically consisted of a proline substitution and thus might produce conformational alterations in BamD that extend beyond residue 188, we then wished to determine whether disruption of the BamDR188–BamAD481 salt bridge was minimally sufficient to provide resistance to MRL-494. Indeed, we found that both the bamDR188D and bamAD481R charge-change mutations conferred the same 2-fold increase in MRL-494 resistance as bamDR188P (Fig. 2C), suggesting that the increase in MRL-494 resistance conferred by bamDR188P is largely due to the disruption of the BamDR188–BamAD481 interaction. It did not escape our attention that residue D481 of BamA is also capable of interacting with residue R29 of BamE (SI Appendix, Fig. S2), as is apparent in numerous structures of the Bam complex solved to date (44). However, introduction of the bamER29D charge-change mutation resulted in no change in the MRL-494 MIC relative to wild-type (Fig. 2C), suggesting that disruption of the BamAD481–BamER29 interaction does not significantly affect MRL-494 resistance. Together, these results demonstrate that disruption of the BamDR188–BamAD481 salt bridge is minimally sufficient to confer resistance to the Bam complex inhibitor MRL-494.

Given that bamAE470K confers both MRL-494 resistance and defects in substrate quality control, we then asked whether mutations in bamD that confer MRL-494 resistance also confer defects in substrate quality control. While strains expressing substrate BamAβ7 in bamDR188P and bamDR188D genetic backgrounds showed only slight reductions in plating efficiency relative to wild-type (SI Appendix, Fig. S3), both bamDR188P and bamDR188D conferred an increased accumulation of substrate BamAβ7 at the BamA lateral gate, as evidenced by an increase in the amount of crosslinked BamAβ7 to residue S439 of assembly machinery BamA (Fig. 2D). Thus, similarly to MRL-494 resistance, disruption of the BamDR188–BamAD481 interaction is minimally sufficient to confer substrate quality control defects. Together, these results reveal the existence of alleles of bamD that confer both resistance to the Bam complex inhibitor MRL-494 and substrate quality control defects, establishing a correlation between these two phenotypes and providing direct evidence that BamD functions in substrate quality control through its direct interaction with BamA.

### Mutations in bamA that bypass BamD activity confer both MRL-494 resistance and defects in substrate quality control

The existence of alleles of bamD that confer both MRL-494 resistance and defects in substrate quality control through their inability to properly interact with BamA argues strongly that bamAE470K confers these two phenotypes as a result of its bypass of BamD function. Thus, bypass of BamD function should be a general predictor of both MRL-494 resistance and defects in substrate quality control. Therefore, we asked whether other alleles of bamA known to be less dependent on BamD activity for viability also confer these two phenotypes. Of particular interest are the bamA alleles bamAF494L and bamAA496P (Fig. 3A), as these mutations are individually sufficient to permit growth under conditions of either greatly reduced or complete removal of BamD, respectively (11, 45). Strains harboring either bamAF494L or bamAA496P at the native bamA locus were constructed and directly compared to the MRL-494-resistant bamAE470K and bamAD481R mutants in MIC assays. We found that both bamAF494L and bamAA496P were individually sufficient to confer 2- and 4-fold increases in MRL-494 resistance, respectively, when expressed from the native bamA chromosomal locus (Fig. 3B). Given that the bamAE470K, bamAF494L, and bamAA496P mutations all permit reductions in BamD activity and confer MRL-494 resistance, we wondered whether the MRL-494-resistant bamAD481R mutant might also be viable under conditions of reduced BamD levels. However, we found that bamAD481R was insufficient to support viability under conditions of BamD depletion (SI Appendix, Fig. S4), at least at the levels of BamD depletion achieved in a plating assay. Thus, as bamAE470K and bamAA496P both permit complete deletion of bamD (11, 12), the ability of bamA alleles to tolerate reductions in BamD activity serves as a general predictor of the magnitude of MRL-494 resistance conferred.

We then asked whether these alleles of bamA that bypass BamD activity and confer MRL-494 resistance are also defective in their ability to perform substrate quality control, as is true for bamAE470K. Indeed, strains expressing substrate BamAβ7 in bamAD481R, bamAF494L, and bamAA496P genetic backgrounds all showed reductions in plating efficiency that correlated with both their ability to tolerate reductions in BamD activity and level of MRL-494 resistance conferred (Fig. 3C). To confirm that the reductions in plating efficiency in bamAE470K, bamAD481R, bamAF494L, and bamAA496P genetic backgrounds were all being conferred through a similar mechanism, we again assessed the accumulation of BamAβ7 at the BamA lateral gate using in vivo photocrosslinking experiments. bamAD481R, bamAF494L, and bamAA496P, like bamAE470K, all produced increased crosslinking of BamAβ7 to residue S439 of assembly machinery BamA relative to wild-type (Fig. 3D), demonstrating that the substrate quality control defects conferred by these four alleles of bamA all occur through the same basic mechanism. Together, these results demonstrate that bypass of BamD activity is a general predictor both MRL-494 resistance and substrate quality control defects. Given the existence of bamD mutations that confer the same two phenotypes through their inability to directly interact with BamA, we conclude that BamD-mediated regulation of BamA functions as a mechanism of substrate quality control during OMP assembly.

### Bypass of BamD activity produces dominant outer membrane permeability defects that are synthetic with Δskp

Given that bypass of BamD activity causes the lethal accumulation of defective OMP substrates on BamA, we wondered whether bypass of BamD activity also imposes significant physiological consequences under native conditions in which all OMP substrates are fully competent to fold. Strikingly, we found that all four alleles of bamA that bypass BamD activity not only confer OM permeability defects in otherwise wild-type genetic backgrounds but do so in a manner that correlates with the degree of toxicity conferred by each allele upon expression of the defective substrate BamAβ7 (Fig. 4A). These increases in OM permeability occurred irrespective of the antibiotic used, as each bamA allele produced similar reductions in plating efficiency on vancomycin, rifampicin, and erythromycin (Fig. 4A)—three small molecules of varied size and hydrophobicity that normally do not easily cross the OM. Crucially, diploid analysis revealed that these OM permeability defects were all conferred in a dominant manner; all four alleles of bamA that bypass BamD activity caused the same relative reductions in plating efficiency regardless of whether a second, wild-type copy of bamA was provided in trans at an ectopic chromosomal locus (attTn7) (Fig. 4A). Thus, the OM permeability defects conferred by bamAE470K, bamAD481R, bamAF494L, and bamAA496P result from the activity of the mutant BamA proteins themselves. As the magnitude of dominant OM permeability observed matches the degree to which each of these four alleles of bamA bypasses BamD activity, these results suggest that BamD-mediated regulation of BamA functions to maintain the integrity of the OM permeability barrier by preventing the uptake of toxic small molecules across the OM.

Because the OM permeability defects caused by bamAE470K, bamAD481R, bamAF494L, and bamAA496P occur under native conditions in which all OMP substrates are fully competent to fold, we asked whether the observed increases in OM permeability were dependent on the presence of the lipoprotein RcsF. The RcsF–OMP complex is a notoriously difficult substrate to assemble, requires both BamA–BamD and BamA–BamE conformational coordination for proper assembly, and represents the only native BamA substrate identified to date that is solely capable of causing a lethal arrest of Bam complex activity (11, 16, 18, 46, 47). However, all four bamA alleles conferred the same relative increases in OM permeability in a ΔrcsF genetic background (SI Appendix, Fig. S5), demonstrating that RcsF does not significantly contribute to the OM permeability defects caused by bamAE470K, bamAD481R, bamAF494L, and bamAA496P. These results are consistent with previous observations that bamAF494L in fact destabilizes the RcsF–BamA complex (48) and thereby prevents the RcsF-dependent lethal arrest of Bam complex assembly that occurs in a bamB bamE double null mutant (9, 46, 47, 49). As even the most phenotypically severe of these four bamA alleles do not appear to be defective in the assembly of any major OMP (11, 49), it seems likely that the defects in OM permeability caused by bamAE470K, bamAD481R, bamAF494L, and bamAA496P are conferred in a general manner, irrespective of any particular BamA substrate.

If the observed OM permeability defects caused by bamA alleles that bypass BamD function are directly due to defects in substrate quality control, there might exist a synthetic genetic interaction between said bamA alleles and skp. In other words, bypassing BamD-mediated substrate quality control through bamAE470K in a strain that lacks skp may result in greater OM permeability defects than the individual effects of either bamAE470K or Δskp alone, thus indicating likely functional overlap of BamD and Skp. We assessed OM permeability by plating bamAE470K, Δskp, and bamAE470K Δskp mutants on media containing the detergent sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), a divalent cation chelator that disrupts the bridging of LPS molecules and sensitizes the OM (2). Importantly, both the bamAE470K and Δskp single mutants showed only slight defects in OM permeability at the concentrations of SDS and EDTA used (Fig. 4B), as was true for the bamAE470K attTn7::bamA merodiploid (Fig. 4B). However, the bamAE470K Δskp double mutant failed to grow at all dilutions plated (Fig. 4B), indicating that the OM permeability defects of the bamAE470K Δskp double mutant are far greater than the effects of either single mutation alone. Notably, expression of a second, wild-type copy of bamA from an ectopic chromosomal locus (attTn7) failed to complement the enhanced OM permeability defects of the bamAE470K Δskp double mutant (Fig. 4B), thus demonstrating that the synthetic OM permeability defects produced by bamAE470K in a Δskp genetic background are conferred in a dominant manner. Moreover, these results indicate that the activity of the Bam complex in the bamAE470K attTn7::bamA merodiploid is defective in a manner that necessitates Skp function. As would be expected, expression of skp from attTn7 (SI Appendix, Fig. S6) in the bamAE470K Δskp double mutant restored plating efficiency to a level comparable to the bamAE470K single mutant (Fig. 4B). Given that bypassing BamD activity through bamAE470K in a strain that lacks skp produces dominant, synthetic defects in OM permeability, BamD and Skp likely have overlapping functions in maintaining OM integrity.

If the synthetic OM permeability defects conferred by bamAE470K in a Δskp genetic background are indeed a result of bypassing BamD function, then a similar synthetic genetic interaction should exist between bamDR188P and Δskp. Therefore, we performed an analogous genetic analysis to assess the OM permeability phenotypes of bamDR188P, Δskp, and bamDR188P Δskp mutants plated on media containing SDS and EDTA. While the bamDR188P single mutant exhibited no OM permeability defects on media containing the same concentrations of SDS and EDTA used for genetic analysis of bamAE470K (Fig. 4C), bamDR188P conferred a further reduction in plating efficiency in a Δskp genetic background (Fig. 4C), thus indicating a synthetic genetic interaction between bamDR188P and Δskp. Crucially, diploid analysis revealed that the enhanced OM permeability defects of the bamDR188P Δskp double mutant could be complemented to levels comparable to the Δskp single mutant through expression of a second, wild-type copy of bamD from attTn7 (Fig. 4C and SI Appendix, Fig. S7). These observations indicate that the increased OM permeability defects conferred by bamDR188P in a Δskp genetic background are recessive and therefore result from the loss of BamD function. Thus, both BamD bypass and the loss of BamD function—both of which, like Δskp, result in defects in substrate quality control—confer synthetic OM permeability defects in the absence of skp. We conclude that the substrate quality control functions performed by both BamD and Skp act to prevent the uptake of toxic small molecules across the OM and thereby maintain the integrity of the OM permeability barrier.

## DISCUSSION

Our previous work showed that the periplasmic chaperone Skp functions to remove stalled OMP substrates from the Bam complex and delivers them to the protease DegP for degradation (38). By clearing these slow-folding OMPs and subsequently facilitating their degradation, Skp ensures both the rapid membrane integration and proper quality control of β-barrel substrates. In this study, we have used assembly-defective substrates to further probe OMP quality control mechanisms and have found that bamAE470K, an allele of bamA that provides resistance to the Bam complex inhibitor MRL-494 and bypasses the essential requirement for BamD (12, 33), phenocopies Δskp and confers substrate quality control defects through the same basic mechanism. Using MRL-494 resistance, we have identified alleles of bamD that phenocopy bamAE470K. These mutations disrupt a single interaction site with BamA and impair substrate quality control in a similar way. Together, our findings support a model in which BamD normally regulates BamA to ensure proper quality control during OMP assembly through a mechanism that functionally overlaps with that of Skp. When BamD is unable to properly interact with and regulate BamA, or when BamA skips BamD-mediated regulation due to a bypass suppressor mutation, this quality control step fails. As a result, OM permeability increases, and cells become sensitized to toxicity caused by stalled defective OMPs that accumulate on BamA.

Overall, we have identified three phenotypic consequences of bypassing BamD-mediated regulation of BamA: loss of proper substrate quality control, resistance to MRL-494, and increased OM permeability. The fact that each of these phenotypes correlates with the degree of BamD bypass carries several implications regarding both BamD function and the mechanism of action of MRL-494, which we discuss below.

It is well established that BamD regulates BamA conformation and that this regulation is essential (11–15). Mutations in bamA that bypass BamD activity must then alter BamA conformation in such a manner that renders BamA less dependent on BamD for conformational coordination during OMP assembly. Indeed, bamAE470K, which most greatly bypasses BamD activity, profoundly alters BamA conformation and destabilizes the BamA β-barrel domain (33). It is clear, however, that the bypass of BamD activity by bamAE470K is not absolute, as deletion of bamD in a bamAE470K genetic background dramatically reduces the efficiency of OMP assembly and greatly weakens OM integrity (4, 11, 12). Given that we have shown that disruption of a single BamA–BamD interaction site is minimally sufficient to produce the same phenotypes that are conferred by bamAE470K, we propose that bamAE470K and other bamA mutations that bypass BamD activity share the fundamental commonality of altering BamA conformation to be less receptive to the conformational changes that are normally promoted by BamD.

MRL-494 inhibits OMP assembly (33), although the molecular mechanism is not yet fully understood. bamAE470K was originally identified as an MRL-494-resistant allele because it improves the efficiency of OMP assembly during MRL-494 treatment (33), but later work revealed its unique ability to bypass BamD essentiality (12). Here, we report bamD alleles that also confer resistance to MRL-494. We further show that the extent to which any given bamA allele can tolerate reduced BamD activity reliably predicts the magnitude of its MRL-494 resistance. Together, these results suggest that MRL-494 inhibits Bam complex function by disrupting the conformational changes in BamA that are normally facilitated by BamD. We propose that MRL-494 resistance fundamentally arises from mutations that make BamA less dependent on BamD for proper conformational coordination.

While our results clearly demonstrate that BamD-mediated regulation of BamA functions as a mechanism of substrate quality control during OMP assembly, we do not yet know how this occurs on a molecular level. It is well-established that the proper binding of unfolded substrates by BamD via the β-signal (13, 20, 22, 39, 50, 51) regulates the conformational changes that promote efficient substrate engagement by BamA (13–15). Importantly, our results show that this BamD-mediated regulation of BamA extends beyond initial substrate recognition and occurs during folding, as BamA substrate C-terminal fragments containing as many as 9 β-strands are effectively prevented from accumulating on BamA by BamD. Thus, the simplest possible mechanism by which BamD-mediated substrate quality control could occur is through promoting substrate disengagement from BamA. We propose that in addition to regulating substrate engagement by BamA (13–15), BamD is also capable of inducing conformational changes in BamA that promote substrate disengagement as a means to enable proper substrate quality control.

We have shown that BamA substrate C-terminal fragments require a minimum of 7 β-strands to confer evident toxicity in the absence of the quality control functions performed by BamD or Skp. Intriguingly, this number of β-strands corresponds to the approximate point in BamA folding in which the first of two stable folding intermediates is observed (23). Moreover, we note that the point at which BamA folding proceeds beyond this first intermediate (23) coincides with the point at which BamA substrate C-terminal fragments begin to confer substantial toxicity even in a wild-type genetic background. These observations not only suggest that the quality control functions performed by both BamD and Skp are especially critical during the stage in folding that encompasses this first stable folding intermediate, but also imply that the completion of folding through this intermediate represents the point at which substrates are no longer subject to these quality control functions.

We do not yet know whether BamD and Skp represent two independent pathways of substrate quality control or if these two proteins function together within a single mechanism. While our data do not definitively exclude the possibility of two separate pathways, we favor the simpler alternative that BamD and Skp perform distinct but complementary functions as part of a single mechanism of substrate quality control. One can readily envision a mechanism in which the regulation of BamA conformation by BamD (13–15) and the high-affinity chaperone activity of Skp (37) could be complementary to one another in facilitating the disengagement of defective substrates from the assembly machinery. We have shown that while both BamD bypass and the deletion of skp produce observable phenotypes, the combined inactivation of both BamD and Skp activity causes synthetic phenotypes that are greater than the loss of either single activity alone. Such a genetic relationship is indeed reminiscent of those exhibited by single and double null mutants of the nonessential lipoproteins of the Bam complex (8, 9, 17, 19, 49) and is thus suggestive of a singular mechanism of substrate quality control.

Through diploid analysis, we have shown that the OM permeability defects that occur as a result of bypassing BamD activity are conferred in a dominant manner. These results demonstrate that the defects in OM permeability result from the activity of the mutant BamA proteins themselves. As BamD bypass both exhibits a synthetic genetic interaction with skp deletion and similarly confers defects in substrate quality control, the simplest possible mechanism consistent with these data is that bypass of BamD activity facilitates the uptake of toxic small molecules across the OM via a membrane pore formed by substrate-engaged BamA. Such a mechanism is not unprecedented, as it has long been known that the slow-folding substrate LptD4213 produces dominant OM permeability defects through its prolonged engagement with BamA (22, 52, 53). Additionally, it has been shown that the BamA lumen forms a translocation channel for the export of extracellular passenger domains across the OM during autotransporter assembly (54), providing further evidence that substrate engagement facilitates transport of molecules across the OM via the BamA lumen. While we indeed favor the simpler mechanism wherein the defects in substrate quality control that occur upon bypassing BamD activity are directly responsible for facilitating the uptake of toxic small molecules through BamA, we cannot definitively exclude the possibility that bypass of BamD activity alone sufficiently alters BamA conformation to enable small molecule uptake through the BamA lumen, irrespective of substrate engagement. Alternatively, it is possible that both the altered BamA conformation and substrate quality control defects that occur as a result of BamD bypass contribute to the BamA-facilitated uptake of toxic small molecules. Nevertheless, we note that the striking magnitude of the synthetic OM permeability defects that occur upon the bypass of BamD activity and removal of Skp strongly suggests the involvement of substrate.

The existence of multiple quality control functions suggests that the cell goes to great lengths to ensure rapid substrate assembly and thereby minimize the time in which BamA exists in the substrate-engaged state. Such functional redundancy is not surprising given the exceptional toxicity of unfolded OMPs (55) and the potential for arrested substrate assembly to result in lethality (11, 16, 18, 46, 47). However, as we have demonstrated that the functions of both BamD and Skp are also important for preventing small molecule uptake across the OM, our results further suggest that substrate quality control functions may have also evolved to prevent the inadvertent uptake of toxic small molecules from the external environment, a process that is likely facilitated by the substrate-engaged state of BamA. It is clear that while both BamD and Skp are individually sufficient to perform some degree of substrate quality control, the combined activities of BamD and Skp enable a far greater tolerance to defects in Bam-catalyzed β-barrel assembly. Nonetheless, this individual sufficiency could indeed explain how diderm bacteria possessing solely BamD or Skp are still able to ensure proper quality control of β-barrel substrates. Intriguingly, the diderm Firmicute Veillonella parvula—which, like most other diderm Terrabacteria, appears to lack OM lipoproteins (56–58) and hence likely lacks BamD—potentially encodes as many as four different Skp proteins (56). Identifying the mechanisms by which diverse organisms ensure the rapid and efficient assembly of β-barrel substrates will provide key insights into the fundamental processes of β-barrel assembly and OM biogenesis in diderm bacteria.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Bacterial Strains and Growth Conditions

All bacterial strains used in this study are listed in SI Appendix, Table S1. Unless otherwise stated, bacterial strains were cultivated aerobically in lysogeny broth (LB) (LB Broth, Lennox; Fisher Scientific) with agitation in a roller drum or on LB agar (1.5% (w/v) agar; Becton, Dickinson and Company) at 37°C. Growth media were supplemented with 50 mg/L ampicillin, 10 mg/L chloramphenicol, 25 mg/L kanamycin, 10 mg/L tetracycline, 0.2% (w/v) L-arabinose, or 0.05% (w/v) D-fucose (Biosynth) as necessary unless otherwise indicated. MRL-494 hydrochloride was purchased from MedChemExpress. All chemicals were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich unless otherwise noted.

### Strain and Plasmid Construction

All strains were constructed using standard microbiological techniques as previously described (59). All plasmids were constructed using Gibson assembly or site-directed mutagenesis (SDM) and confirmed by sequencing. All oligonucleotides (Integrated DNA Technologies) used in this study are listed in SI Appendix, Tables S2 and S3. Deletion alleles originated from the Keio collection (60) and, when necessary, kanamycin resistance cassettes were excised using the FLP recombinase as previously described (61). Tn10 insertion alleles originated from the Carol Gross Tn10 mapping collection (62). bamADE alleles were introduced at their native chromosomal loci through recombineering using CspRecT as previously described (63). Construction of the attTn7::bamA and λatt::ParaBAD-surA integration constructs and the BamD-depletion strain has been previously described (10, 46, 64).

Wild-type alleles of skp and bamD were inserted at the Tn7 attachment site (attTn7) as previously described (65) with minor modifications. Briefly, skp and its native promoter (defined as 200 base pairs (bp) upstream of skp) or bamD and its native promoter (defined as 300 bp upstream of bamD) were amplified by PCR and inserted into the mini-Tn7 suicide vector pUC18R6KT-mini-Tn7T-Km by Gibson assembly. Exponentially growing cells harboring tnsABCD on pBAD18 were induced with a final concentration of 0.2% arabinose for 15 min and transformed with the mini-Tn7 suicide vector containing either skp or bamD by electroporation. Proper transposition of the integration constructs into attTn7 was confirmed by PCR and sequencing, and the integrated attTn7::skp and attTn7::bamD constructs were moved into the appropriate genetic backgrounds by P1vir transduction.

A single codon mutant library of bamD was constructed using SDM covering all residues except for the signal sequence (24–245). For this, partially overlapping (15-bp overlap) primers (SI Appendix, Table S3) were used to allow self-annealing of a PCR product and direct transformation into E. coli cells, where it can be ligated by host repair enzymes. The primers encode an NNK (where N = A/C/G/T, K = G/T) diversified codon. pZS21::bamD (17) was used as a template to PCR amplify the plasmid with the corresponding primers using Q5 High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (New England Biolabs). The purified PCR products were subjected to DpnI digestion (New England Biolabs), and the entire reaction was transformed into E. coli Mach1 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with recovery in SOC medium (2% (w/v) tryptone, 0.5% (w/v) yeast extract, 10 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 10 mM MgSO4, and 20 mM glucose) for 1 h at 37°C. Then, about 100 μL of 25% of codon pools were plated to estimate library diversity based on colony count and select colony sequencing. Kanamycin was added to the remaining cultures, and transformants were selected by growing in liquid culture overnight. While this library is not built for saturation, at least 70% of codons were estimated to be mutagenized with at least one non-synonymous substitution.

### Efficiency of Plating Assay

Strains were grown overnight at 37°C unless otherwise indicated. Overnight cultures were 10-fold serially diluted and plated onto the indicated LB agar media using a 48-pin replicator. The resulting plates were incubated overnight at 37°C unless otherwise noted. For plating assays of strains expressing BamA substrate C-terminal fragments or full-length BamA from pBAD18, bacteria were grown overnight at 30°C, 10-fold serially diluted, plated onto LB agar containing 200 mg/L ampicillin and either 0.05% fucose or 0.2% arabinose, and incubated at 30°C.

### SDS-PAGE and Immunoblotting

SDS-PAGE was performed using 8% or 10% hand-cast polyacrylamide gels with Tris-glycine-SDS running buffer. Proteins were transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes (Amersham Protran; Cytiva) using a semidry transfer system (Trans-Blot Turbo; Bio-Rad). Immunoblotting was performed using a mouse monoclonal antibody recognizing FLAG (1:5,000 dilution; Sigma-Aldrich) or a rabbit polyclonal antibody recognizing GroEL (1:80,000 dilution; Sigma-Aldrich). Goat anti-mouse IgG–peroxidase (1:3,000 dilution; Bio-Rad) or goat anti-rabbit IgG–peroxidase (1:10,000 dilution; Sigma-Aldrich) secondary antibodies were used for all immunoblots. Immunoblots were developed using a chemiluminescent Western HRP substrate (Immobilon Crescendo or Immobilon Classico; Millipore) and imaged using the ChemiDoc XRS+ system (Bio-Rad).

### In Vivo Site-Specific Photocrosslinking

Strains harboring pSup-BpaRS-6TRN (42), pBAD18::bamAβ7, and the indicated pZS21::bamAS439Am variants were grown overnight in a roller drum at 30°C, diluted 1:50 into 7 mL LB supplemented with 0.8 mM pBpa (Bachem) and 100 ng/mL anhydrotetracycline (Takara Bio), and incubated in a roller drum at 37°C until an OD600 of about 0.8–1.0 was reached. A final concentration of 0.2% arabinose was then added to induce BamAβ7 expression and the resulting cultures were incubated for 2 min in a shaking water bath at 37°C. The cultures were then chilled for 5 min in an ice bath, collected by centrifugation (1,200 × g, 10 min, 4°C), and concentrated to an OD600 of 10 in ice-cold 1× phosphate-buffered saline (pH 7.4). An aliquot of each culture was directly irradiated with UV light (3UV-38 UV lamp; UVP) at 365 nm for 16 min at 4°C while a second aliquot was left untreated on ice at 4°C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (16,100 × g, 2 min, 4°C) and resuspended in 2× Laemmli sample buffer (Bio-Rad) containing 10% (v/v) β-mercaptoethanol to a concentration equivalent to an OD600 of 28. Samples were boiled for 10 min, centrifuged (16,100 × g, 2 min, room temperature) to pellet insoluble material, and analyzed by SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting as described above.

### Screen for MRL-494-Resistant bamD Mutants

Screens for MRL-494-resistant bamD mutants were performed as previously described for bamA (33). Briefly, the BamD-depletion strain (10) was transformed with bamD NNK mutagenesis library plasmid pools and grown in the absence of arabinose to deplete chromosomally encoded BamD. The BamD-depletion strain transformed with wild-type, plasmid-encoded BamD served as a control. The bamD mutant library was treated with 2-fold serial dilutions of MRL-494 at final concentrations ranging from 4-fold higher than the MIC to 512-fold lower than the MIC in a 96-well plate and incubated overnight at 37°C. Cells growing at or above the MRL-494 MIC (25 μM; (33)) were harvested and plasmid-borne bamD alleles were identified by sequencing. Alleles of interest were rebuilt by SDM and assessed using the same assay prior to being introduced at the native bamD chromosomal locus.

### Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) Assay

Exponentially growing cultures of the indicated strains were diluted 1:1,000 into a 96-well plate and treated with MRL-494 at final concentrations ranging from 4-fold higher than the MIC to 8-fold lower than the MIC in 2-fold increments. The plate was sealed with a breathable membrane (Breathe-Easy; Sigma-Aldrich) and incubated with orbital shaking at 37°C for about 24 h.
